passage:
Dolma: I just sent my cousin a 400-word congratulations message for her new job in Canada
Yogesh: that's... a lot of words 😄
Dolma: I know. I've also liked every single photo. and offered to help her pack. twice
Yogesh: are you ok?
Dolma: honestly? I think I'm jealous. I applied abroad too and got nothing
Dolma: and I'm also really happy for her. both
Yogesh: both is allowed
Dolma: it feels better saying it. like I don't have to perform anymore
Yogesh: so what now
Dolma: I'll still help her pack. but because I want to, not to prove I'm not jealous 🙂

qa.q: Where is the cousin's new job?
qa.a: In Canada.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling under the extra-nice messages?
qa.a: Jealous, having applied abroad without success, and also truly happy for the cousin.

qa.q: What changed once Dolma admitted both feelings?
qa.a: Dolma stopped performing; helping the cousin pack became genuine instead of a way to prove there was no jealousy.

qa.q: How might the cousin experience Dolma's help now?
qa.a: As warm and real, without the slightly overdone edge of a 400-word message.

grounding: An adult notices overdone niceness toward a cousin, admits being both envious and happy, and the kindness becomes genuine.

passage: In the small town of Bagalkot, Urmila's new tailoring shop had opened opposite Jahnavi's, and within a month half of Jahnavi's customers had crossed the road. Jahnavi found herself taking Urmila sweets every other day, praising her stitching to everyone, laughing a little too loudly at her jokes. One evening, walking home past the temple, she caught herself rehearsing yet another compliment, and stopped. "I'm jealous," she said quietly to the dark road. "And I actually like her." Saying both made her chest loosen. The next morning she didn't take sweets. She went across and said, "Your blouse designs are better than mine. Teach me that neckline? I'll teach you my hemming." Urmila grinned and pulled up a stool.

qa.q: How quickly did half of Jahnavi's customers cross the road?
qa.a: Within a month.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel when she stopped on the road?
qa.a: She admitted she felt jealous of Urmila and also that she liked her; saying both made her chest loosen with relief.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do differently the next morning?
qa.a: Instead of sweets and overdone praise, she honestly admired Urmila's designs and offered to swap skills.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about the skill swap?
qa.a: Pleased and welcomed, grinning and pulling up a stool, glad of a real friend across the road.

grounding: An adult notices overdone niceness toward a rival, admits being envious and fond at once, and her kindness becomes genuine.

passage: When Gabriel won the research fellowship in Lyon that Nour had also wanted, she became his biggest fan. She organised his farewell dinner, planned a speech, and bought him an expensive notebook. Her flatmate said, "You're being so generous." Nour smiled, but lying awake that night, she felt a knot in her stomach. She wrote in her journal: "I'm envious. I wanted it. And I'm glad it's him, because he's kind." Both were true. By morning the knot was gone. At the dinner, her speech was shorter and warmer than she had planned. She told Gabriel, "I'm jealous, you know. And I'm proud of you." He laughed and hugged her. "That's the nicest thing anyone's said."

qa.q: What did Nour buy Gabriel?
qa.a: An expensive notebook.

qa.q: What feeling was behind the knot in Nour's stomach?
qa.a: Envy she hadn't admitted; she wanted the fellowship, and the extra generosity was covering it.

qa.q: How did writing in her journal help?
qa.a: Admitting both envy and gladness loosened the knot and made her speech shorter, warmer and genuine.

qa.q: How did Gabriel react to Nour's honesty?
qa.a: He laughed, hugged her, and called it the nicest thing anyone had said, clearly touched.

grounding: An adult catches herself overdoing kindness to a rival, admits envy alongside gladness, and the kindness becomes real.

subtype: Baby talk after a new sibling [Actor]
passage: Class note, Diwali week. Hemant's baby brother, Omkar, was born last month. Since then Hemant has started talking like a baby at school: "Me want milk," "Hemant tired, carry." He had two accidents this week, though he has been dry for a year, and he cried when his mother left at drop-off, clinging to her dupatta. I think he wants to know he will still be looked after. I gave him a special helper job and extra lap time at story hour. I have shared this with his parents and suggested some one-to-one time with him at home.

qa.q: When was Omkar born?
qa.a: Last month.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling when he talks like a baby?
qa.a: Unsure and a little left out since the baby came, wanting to be sure there is still room for him to be looked after.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond?
qa.a: Gave him a special helper job and extra lap time, and suggested one-to-one time at home, without scolding.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother feel at drop-off?
qa.a: Torn and tender, with a new baby at home and a clinging older son.

grounding: A preschooler goes back to baby talk, accidents and clinging after his brother is born.

subtype: Baby talk after a new sibling [Actor]
passage: In the harvest season, when baby Rehana came home to the village, everyone crowded around her. Nitin, who had drunk from a steel tumbler for two years, suddenly wanted a bottle "like baby". He crawled instead of walking, said "goo-goo" at dinner, and clung to Amma's leg while she fed Rehana. Dadi laughed at first, then saw his eyes. She pulled him onto her lap. "You want to be small again, na? So Amma looks at you too." Nitin nodded into her shoulder. That evening Amma handed Rehana to Dadi and took Nitin to see the paddy stacks, just the two of them.

qa.q: What had Nitin drunk from for two years?
qa.a: A steel tumbler.

qa.q: Why did Nitin want a bottle like the baby's?
qa.a: He felt left out and worried there was no room for him, so acting small was a way to be looked at and cared for.

qa.q: What did Dadi and Amma do right?
qa.a: Dadi named his wish kindly instead of laughing, and Amma spent time alone with him at the paddy stacks.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to have Nitin clinging while she feeds Rehana?
qa.a: She is probably stretched and tired, and relieved when Dadi helps her give Nitin time.

grounding: A child goes back to a bottle, crawling and clinging after his baby sister is born.

subtype: Baby talk after a new sibling [Actor]
passage: In the dark winter weeks after baby Anders was born, Aiko stopped using full sentences. "Aiko want up," she whined, arms raised, though she had been telling long stories all autumn. She asked for her old dummy and wet her bed twice. Her father, busy with the baby, felt his patience wearing thin. Then he noticed her watching him rock Anders, her thumb in her mouth. He put the baby in the cot, sat on the floor, and pulled Aiko into his lap. "You're still my big girl," he said, "and you can be little with me too." She snuggled in. The next morning she told him a whole story about snow bears.

qa.q: How many times did Aiko wet her bed?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What might Aiko have been feeling as she watched her father rock Anders?
qa.a: Left out and anxious, wanting to know there was still room for her to be cuddled.

qa.q: What did her father do that helped?
qa.a: Instead of losing patience, he put the baby down, held Aiko, and told her she could be both big and little with him.

qa.q: How did Aiko's father feel at first?
qa.a: Busy and stretched thin, with his patience wearing out before he noticed her need.

grounding: A preschooler returns to baby talk and bedwetting after her brother's birth, looking for reassurance.

subtype: Wanting to sleep near parents after a move [Actor]
passage:
First week in Chennai, humid June: Hemant, who has made his own bed since he was six, leaves it messy every day. At night he drags his pillow into his parents' room. "Just tonight," he says.
Third week: Hemant still sleeps on the floor beside his parents' bed. He hasn't packed his school bag once. His elder brother Jatin teases, "Baby!" Hemant cries.
Sixth week: Amma stops Jatin's teasing and makes Hemant a small corner in his own room, with a night lamp and Nani's old shawl from Jaipur. She sits with him for ten minutes each night. Slowly Hemant goes back to his own bed, and one morning he makes it without being asked.

qa.q: What did Amma put in Hemant's corner?
qa.a: A night lamp and Nani's old shawl from Jaipur.

qa.q: Why did Hemant start sleeping in his parents' room?
qa.a: The move to a new city and school made him anxious and unsettled, so he reached for the early comfort of being near his parents.

qa.q: What helped Hemant return to his own bed?
qa.a: Amma stopping the teasing, making a cosy corner with familiar things, and sitting with him each night.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been thinking when he teased Hemant?
qa.a: Probably that Hemant was being silly, not realising how unsettled the move had made him.

grounding: A boy who moved cities goes back to sleeping near his parents and drops his chores until warmth and time help.

subtype: Wanting to sleep near parents after a move [Actor]
passage: Salma, you've been sleeping in your mother's room since you moved here, haven't you? Don't be shy. When your Jeevan appooppan was eight, my family moved from our village to Bombay in the middle of the monsoon. Everything was loud: trains, rain, strangers. I stopped feeding the hens, because we had no hens. I stopped doing anything. And every night I crept to my mother's mat and slept pressed against her back. My father said, "He's too old for this." My mother said, "He's not too old. He's scared." She let me stay, and she gave me a job: watering the tulsi on the balcony. By Diwali, I was back on my own mat.

qa.q: What job did his mother give young Jeevan?
qa.a: Watering the tulsi on the balcony.

qa.q: Why did young Jeevan creep to his mother's mat?
qa.a: He was scared and overwhelmed by the loud new city, and being close to her felt safe.

qa.q: What choice by his mother helped him move forward?
qa.a: She let him stay without shaming him and gave him a small job, so he felt safe and useful until he was ready.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's father see his behaviour?
qa.a: He thought Jeevan was too old for it, while his mother saw that he was scared.

grounding: An elder recalls how, after moving cities as a child, he slept beside his mother and dropped his chores until he felt safe.

subtype: Wanting to sleep near parents after a move [Actor]
passage: The move from Amritsar to Pune happened in December, into a two-room flat where boxes were still piled to the ceiling. Gurleen, nine, stopped folding her clothes and stopped feeding the fish, jobs she had loved. Every night she said her tummy hurt and asked to sleep between Mummy and Papa. The bed was small, Papa had an early shift, and her little sister Hansa wanted the same thing. One night Mummy sat with both girls on the mattress in their room. "New places are scary. Your bodies want to be close. So for two weeks, I'll sit here till you sleep." Gurleen held her hand. By the third week she was feeding the fish again, without being asked.

qa.q: Which jobs did Gurleen stop doing?
qa.a: Folding her clothes and feeding the fish.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say her tummy hurt at night?
qa.a: She felt anxious and unsettled after the move and wanted the comfort of being close to her parents.

qa.q: What did Mummy do, given the small flat?
qa.a: She sat with both girls in their room until they slept for two weeks, saying new places are scary, instead of refusing or scolding.

qa.q: How might Hansa be affected by the move?
qa.a: She also feels unsettled and wants the same closeness, and Mummy's plan helps her too.

grounding: A child who moved cities drops her chores and wants to sleep near her parents until warmth helps her settle.

passage: At the sports hostel in Thiruvananthapuram, the state team list went up on Friday, and Gopika's name wasn't on it. She went straight to her room and got under the blanket. She didn't go to dinner. She didn't answer her roommate Himani. On Saturday she asked only for the rice kanji her grandmother used to make when she was a sick little girl. Himani told the warden, who didn't lecture. The warden brought kanji from the mess kitchen, with pickle, and sat on the next bed without speaking. On Sunday afternoon Gopika sat up, ate a second bowl, and said, "I really wanted it." The warden nodded. "I know. Take today. Tomorrow we'll look at next year."

qa.q: What food did Gopika ask for?
qa.a: The rice kanji her grandmother used to make when she was sick.

qa.q: Why did Gopika stay under the blanket?
qa.a: She felt crushed and ashamed at not being selected, and retreated to be soothed like a little child.

qa.q: What did the warden do that worked?
qa.a: Didn't lecture, brought the kanji, sat quietly nearby, and let her have a day before talking about next year.

qa.q: How might Himani feel when Gopika won't answer?
qa.a: Worried and a bit helpless, which is why she told the warden.

grounding: A teenager who failed a selection trial retreats to bed and childhood food, and warmth and time help her recover.

passage:
Dear Imran,
You asked why I didn't reply all week. I didn't get into the music academy. The result came on Sunday, and I spent three days in bed with the curtains shut. I didn't want to talk to anyone, not even Ammi. All I wanted was the sweet vermicelli she made when I was small, and old cartoons. I felt like a little kid again. On Thursday Ammi just sat on my bed with a bowl and stroked my hair. She didn't say "try again" or "it's fine". That helped more than anything. Today I opened the curtains and played the piano for ten minutes. Not well. But I played.
Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila want to eat?
qa.a: The sweet vermicelli Ammi made when Sharmila was small.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel after the result?
qa.a: Deeply disappointed and small, like a little kid again, wanting only comfort food, cartoons and the curtains shut.

qa.q: What helped Sharmila most?
qa.a: Ammi sitting with a bowl and stroking Sharmila's hair without saying "try again" or "it's fine".

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt during those three days?
qa.a: Worried but patient, choosing quiet comfort over advice.

grounding: A teenager who failed an audition retreats to bed and childhood comforts, and warmth helps them return.

passage: You want to know what I did after the district trials, Usha? Nothing. That's what. I'm Tushar, and I'd been training for two years, and when my name wasn't on the list, I went home, pulled the blanket over my head, and didn't come out for most of a weekend. I didn't answer calls. I didn't want to talk. The only thing I asked Ma for was the khichdi she used to make when I had chickenpox as a kid. Embarrassing, right? But Ma just made it. No speeches. Baba sat outside my door reading the newspaper aloud, bad jokes and all. By Monday I was out of bed. By Wednesday I was back at the nets. Turns out I just needed to be small for a bit.

qa.q: What did Tushar ask Ma for?
qa.a: The khichdi she used to make when Tushar had chickenpox as a kid.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling that weekend?
qa.a: Crushed and ashamed after two years of training, wanting to hide and be comforted.

qa.q: What did Ma and Baba do that helped?
qa.a: Ma made the khichdi without speeches, and Baba sat nearby reading aloud; their warmth let Tushar recover in time.

qa.q: How might Baba have felt sitting outside the door?
qa.a: Worried but patient, wanting to be close without pushing.

grounding: A teenager who failed a selection trial retreats to bed and childhood food, and warmth and time help.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
"You called your mum again, Kalyani?"
"Third time today, Yusuf. I know."
"Hey, no judgement."
"I cried on the phone because the mess ran out of curd. Curd!"
"Exams start Monday. It's not about the curd."
"I feel like I'm twelve. I even asked her to sing me my old lullaby."
"Did she?"
"Yes. Badly. It helped."
"Then it's not weakness. It's what you need right now."
"My roommate talks to her parents once a week."
"Maybe she'll need them more later. And maybe you'll call less by second semester."
"You think?"
"I called home every night last year. Now it's Sundays."

qa.q: Why did Kalyani cry on the phone?
qa.a: Because the mess ran out of curd.

qa.q: How does Kalyani feel about calling home so often?
qa.a: Embarrassed and young, like a twelve-year-old, even though the lullaby helped.

qa.q: How does Yusuf help Kalyani see it?
qa.a: He says it isn't weakness but what Kalyani needs right now, and shares that he called every night last year and now calls only on Sundays.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's mother feel singing the lullaby?
qa.a: Probably tender and glad to comfort Kalyani, even from far away.

grounding: A first-year hostel student calls home often and feels younger during exams, and a friend offers reassurance that comfort is a need.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage: In my first year at college in Delhi, far from Gangtok, I called my mother every single night. During exams, twice. Sometimes I just cried and she listened. I asked her to describe what she was cooking, in detail, like a bedtime story. My friend Akash from the hostel teased me once, and I felt so ashamed that I didn't call for three days, and those were my worst days. When I finally called again, Ama said, "Needing me isn't weakness, Dolma." I believed her. By the second year, something shifted without my noticing. I called on Sundays. I cooked her recipes myself. Now I'm the one my juniors come to when they're homesick.

qa.q: How often did Dolma call during exams?
qa.a: Twice a night.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel after Akash's teasing?
qa.a: So ashamed that Dolma stopped calling for three days, which became the worst days.

qa.q: What did Dolma's mother say, and why did it help?
qa.a: "Needing me isn't weakness," which let Dolma accept comfort until confidence grew on its own.

qa.q: How might Akash have seen Dolma's calls?
qa.a: As something to tease, probably without realising how much Dolma needed them.

grounding: A first-year far from home calls a parent every night and acts younger during exams, and the need eases as confidence grows.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage: Warden's note, November. Jatin in Room 22 calls his mother at least twice a day, and he cried on the phone in the corridor during mid-terms. His roommate Vaibhav mentioned it, worried. Jatin has also been sleeping with his old school hoodie and asking the mess for "home-style" dal. None of this worries me by itself. He attends classes, eats, and is making friends. I told Jatin that calling home is fine and that many first-years do it. I have paired him with Vaibhav for the Sunday walking group, and I will check in after exams. I expect the calls to ease as he settles.

qa.q: What does Jatin sleep with?
qa.a: His old school hoodie.

qa.q: What might Jatin be feeling during mid-terms?
qa.a: Homesick and stressed, reaching for comforts from home like a younger child.

qa.q: What did the warden do, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Reassured Jatin that calling home is fine, paired him with Vaibhav for the Sunday walk, and planned a check-in, without treating the need as weakness.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about Jatin's crying?
qa.a: Worried enough to mention it to the warden.

grounding: A first-year hostel student calls home often and seeks childhood comforts during exams, and a warden treats it as a normal need.

passage:
Dear Amma,
Quick update on Chinnu. Since the baby came, he has started talking in a baby voice and wants to be fed by hand again. My first instinct was to say, "You're a big boy now, stop it." Then I remembered how you handled me when my sister was born: extra cuddles, no teasing, the same bedtime every night. So that's what we're doing. I feed him by hand at dinner if he asks, but bath, story and lights-out stay exactly the same. Yesterday he told me, in his normal voice, "Appa, I'm the big brother." I nearly cried. Thank you for showing me how.
Pradeep

qa.q: What does Chinnu want at dinner?
qa.a: To be fed by hand again.

qa.q: What was Pradeep's first instinct, and how did he feel later?
qa.a: To say "You're a big boy now, stop it"; later he felt so moved that he nearly cried when Chinnu said he was the big brother.

qa.q: How is Pradeep handling the regression?
qa.a: With extra cuddles and hand-feeding when asked, no teasing, and bath, story and lights-out kept the same.

qa.q: How might Chinnu feel with this approach?
qa.a: Reassured that there is still room for him, so he can move forward and call himself the big brother.

grounding: A parent meets a child's baby-like behaviour with patience and cuddles while keeping routines steady.

passage: Anjali, you asked how we got through the months after the move. Honestly? My daughter went backwards. Five years old and suddenly wetting the bed, sucking her thumb, wanting to be carried everywhere. I'm Aditi, and I'll admit my first thought was, "Not now, I'm exhausted." But I remembered my own Nani saying: when a child goes small, make yourself big and soft. So I did. Extra lap time, no scolding about the sheets, songs from when she was a baby. And I didn't change anything else. Same school drop, same dinner time, same bedtime story. It took about six weeks. One day she walked into school without looking back. I cried in the car, the happy kind.

qa.q: How long did it take?
qa.a: About six weeks.

qa.q: What was Aditi's first thought when the daughter went backwards?
qa.a: "Not now, I'm exhausted": Aditi felt tired and stretched thin.

qa.q: What did Aditi do that worked?
qa.a: Extra lap time, no scolding about the sheets and baby songs, while keeping school drop, dinner and bedtime exactly the same.

qa.q: How might the daughter have felt with this approach?
qa.a: Safe and reassured, until she could walk into school without looking back.

grounding: A parent meets a child's regression after a move with warmth and patience while keeping routines steady.

passage: I live across the corridor from Manoj and his son Zubin, and I've watched them these past weeks. Zubin's mother is away caring for her sick father, and since she left, Zubin, who is six, has been talking like a toddler and refusing to walk to the lift. I expected Manoj to lose his temper; he works long shifts. Instead I see him carry Zubin down the stairs every morning, singing silly songs. I've never once heard him say "act your age". Every evening, at exactly seven, their lights dim for the story. I can't know what the boy feels, but yesterday Zubin walked to the lift on his own and waved at me.

qa.q: At what time do their lights dim each evening?
qa.a: At exactly seven.

qa.q: What might Zubin be feeling since his mother left?
qa.a: Unsettled and missing her, so he acts younger to be carried and cared for.

qa.q: What does Manoj do that helps?
qa.a: He carries Zubin with silly songs, never says "act your age", and keeps story time at seven every evening.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Manoj's approach?
qa.a: The narrator seems surprised and quietly admiring, having expected impatience.

grounding: A father meets his son's baby-like behaviour with patience and cuddles while keeping routines steady.

passage:
Monday of Navratri week: Payal's parents argue loudly in the kitchen. Payal stomps up to the terrace, grabs the dhol her uncle left there, and beats it until her arms ache. The neighbour's dog howls.
Wednesday: Another argument. This time Payal goes straight to the terrace. She tries to copy the rhythm from garba practice, fast, then faster. Her anger comes out as a beat. Her friend Hafsa hears it and climbs up to listen.
Saturday: At the colony garba, the drummer lets Payal play for one song. The crowd claps. Afterwards Payal tells Mummy, "When you and Papa shout, I drum." Mummy is quiet, then hugs her. "We'll try to shout less. And you keep drumming."

qa.q: Who left the dhol on the terrace?
qa.a: Payal's uncle.

qa.q: Why did Payal beat the dhol until her arms ached?
qa.a: She felt angry and upset about her parents' argument, and drumming let the anger out safely.

qa.q: What makes drumming a good outlet for Payal?
qa.a: It turns the anger into skill and rhythm, safely, and gives her something she can share.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel when Payal says she drums when they shout?
qa.a: Moved and a bit guilty, realising how the arguments affect Payal, and she hugs her.

grounding: A girl furious about her parents' quarrel bangs a drum until her anger becomes rhythm.

passage: Tanuja, you ran round the building five times after your parents argued, didn't you? Your Pranav mama did the same, at eleven. It was Onam, and my father and uncle had a terrible fight at the sadya, shouting over the banana leaves. I couldn't stand it. I ran out to the paddy field bund and ran, round and round, until my legs shook. The next day I did it again. My games teacher saw me and said, "You're fast when you're angry. Want to train properly?" I trained every evening. Running was where my anger went, instead of into my fists. I won the district 800 metres the next year. But beta, I also needed someone to talk to about the fights. Running was only half of it.

qa.q: Where did young Pranav run?
qa.a: Round the paddy field bund.

qa.q: Why did young Pranav run until his legs shook?
qa.a: He was furious and upset about the shouting at the sadya, and running let the anger out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: His games teacher offering to train him, which turned angry running into skilled practice, though he also needed someone to talk to.

qa.q: How might the games teacher have seen young Pranav?
qa.a: As a fast, angry boy with potential, whose energy needed a proper channel.

grounding: An elder recalls turning anger about a family quarrel into running laps, which became disciplined training.

passage: The winter holidays in their one-room flat meant nowhere to escape when Ammi and Abbu argued. The walls were thin, and it was too cold and foggy to go out. One evening, when the shouting started again, Samir's fists clenched. His sister Pallavi saw it. "Come," she said, grabbing the skipping rope. On the stairwell landing, under the flickering bulb, Samir skipped: fifty, a hundred, two hundred, faster and faster, counting out loud until the counting drowned out the voices. His breath came hard. The anger drained into his legs. When they went back inside, the argument had stopped. Samir set himself a target: five hundred skips by the end of the holidays.

qa.q: What did Pallavi grab?
qa.a: The skipping rope.

qa.q: What did Samir feel when the shouting started?
qa.a: Angry and helpless, his fists clenching.

qa.q: Why was skipping a helpful choice in the small flat?
qa.a: It gave the anger a safe, skilled outlet in a tiny space, and a target to work toward.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel helping Samir?
qa.a: Protective and caring, noticing his clenched fists and offering him a safe way out.

grounding: A boy furious about his parents' quarrels skips rope until the anger drains away, turning it into skill.

passage: When Akash told me in Class 11 that he "only saw me as a friend", I wanted to do something dramatic. Delete his number, post something mean, tell everyone his secrets. I didn't. I went home and wrote a poem instead, a bad one, about a door closing. Then another. For three weeks I filled a notebook. Some poems were angry, some just sad. The words gave the feeling edges, somewhere to stand. In December I read one at the school poetry evening without saying who it was about. A girl from Class 9 came up afterwards and said, "That's exactly how I feel." I'm Bhavna. I still have that notebook. The door poem is still bad. I love it anyway.

qa.q: What was Bhavna's first poem about?
qa.a: A door closing.

qa.q: What did Bhavna want to do at first, and what was Bhavna feeling?
qa.a: Something dramatic, like posting something mean; Bhavna felt hurt and angry after the rejection.

qa.q: How did writing help Bhavna?
qa.a: It gave the hurt edges and shape instead of lashing out, and later let others connect with it at the poetry evening.

qa.q: How did the girl from Class 9 respond?
qa.a: She felt understood, saying, "That's exactly how I feel."

grounding: A teenager who has been rejected writes poems instead of lashing out, giving the hurt a shape others can see.

passage: Music teacher's note, Term 2. Suraj has been bringing me songs almost every day this month. He told me quietly that a girl had turned him down. His friend Avni mentioned that he had been tempted to send the girl something nasty. Instead he has written six songs. The early ones are raw and angry; the newest is gentler, about walking home in the rain. I told him the feeling has found a good home. With his permission, he will play one at the talent show. I will keep an eye on him and check that he is also talking to someone, not only writing.

qa.q: How many songs has Suraj written?
qa.a: Six.

passage: Last season I coached a boxer named Siddharth who had the worst temper in the gym. After his father walked out on the family, he stopped shouting and started training: six a.m. runs, two sessions a day, extra rounds on the bag until his knuckles were raw.
